place.zh: 沂中医 · 体育馆 · 十一月

setup.zh: 院系杯小组赛，他抢到头一个篮板，落地崴了右脚。「疼和伤，是两本账。」阿禾单脚闭眼站给他看：崴过脚的，都得练这个。
setup.en: The group stage of the cup: his first rebound, and he lands on his right ankle. "Pain and injury are two different accounts." Ahe stands on one foot, eyes shut, to show him: everyone who sprains an ankle has to do this.

recap.zh: 崴了右踝；「疼和伤，是两本账」；单脚闭眼，三秒。
recap.en: A sprained right ankle; "pain and injury are two accounts"; one foot, eyes shut, three seconds.

en: One foot, eyes shut: three seconds.

story.zh:
十一月二十五日夜里十一点，沈芒看着马桶里一泡可乐色的尿，头一个念头不是要死了，是：不许让阿禾知道。

这句话，四天前他就在手机备忘录里写下了，还加了粗。

事情得从一只崴了的脚说起。

十一月十四日，院系杯小组赛第二轮，针推对护理。阿禾说话算话，给了他五分钟。他抢到了院系杯生涯的头一个篮板——跟着一群比他高半个头的人一齐跳，竟叫他摸着了——落地时右脚却踩在了人家脚面上，脚踝往外一翻，「咯」的一声，他自己都听见了。他抱着球坐在地上，球还死死攥着。站中锋的大刘后来说，那是他整场打得最好的一下：倒了，球没丢。

校医捏了捏，说外踝韧带拉伤，开了护踝和一对拐。沈芒问：「几天能好？」校医道：「一两个礼拜左右就不疼了。但完全恢复，至少需要三个月。」

沈芒只听进去了前一句，算了一笔账：第三轮在一个礼拜以后，不疼就能上。回宿舍的路上，他瞥见阿禾在本子上他那一行底下添了一句：「第三轮：不上。」

礼拜二针灸实验课散了，他蹭到讲台边，撩起裤腿，露出那只肿得像发面馒头的脚踝：「严老师，您给我这儿扎两针，礼拜六能上场吗？」

严老师看了很久，回身在黑板上写了一行：「所言节者，神气之所游行出入也，非皮肉筋骨也。」「《灵枢》头一篇。扎针，能让你少疼一点，不能让你这根筋长得快一点。疼和伤，是两本账。你那根筋，得它自己长。」

那天晚上，阿禾上六楼送绷带。她把绷带往桌上一扔，抬起一只脚，闭上眼，单脚站在水泥地上，纹丝不动：「崴过脚的，都得练这个。韧带长得慢，比肉慢多了。而且一崴，管脚的那些神经也伤了，脑子不知道脚踩在哪儿，所以老崴。每天闭着眼单脚站，站到一分钟不晃。」

他扶着桌沿试了一回。一闭眼，整个人像插在烂泥里的竹竿，两只胳膊在半空里乱划，第三秒上，好脚「啪」地踩实了地。

「三秒。」阿禾道。
story.en:
At eleven o'clock on the night of November 25th, Shen Mang stared at a stream of cola-colored urine in the toilet, and his first thought was not that he was dying. It was: Ahe must not find out.

He had typed that sentence into the notes on his phone four days earlier, and made it bold.

It all started with a twisted ankle.

November 14th, second round of the group stage in the inter-college cup: Acupuncture and Tuina against Nursing. Ahe was as good as her word and gave him five minutes. He grabbed the first rebound of his inter-college career — he went up with a crowd of people half a head taller than him and somehow got a hand to it — but when he came down, his right foot landed on someone else's, his ankle rolled outward, and there was a "crack" that even he could hear. He sat on the floor hugging the ball, still clutching it tight. Big Liu, who played center, said later it was the best thing he did all game: he went down, and he didn't lose the ball.

The school doctor squeezed it, said lateral ankle ligament strain, and gave him an ankle brace and a pair of crutches. Shen Mang asked, "How many days till it's better?" The doctor said, "The pain should go in a week or two. But a full recovery takes at least three months."

Shen Mang only heard the first half. He only did the sums: the third round was a week away, and once it stopped hurting he could play. On the way back to the dorm, he glimpsed Ahe adding a line under his row in her notebook: "Round three: sits out."

On Tuesday, when acupuncture lab let out, he edged up to the lectern, rolled up his trouser leg, and showed an ankle swollen like a risen steamed bun: "Teacher Yan, if you put a couple of needles in here, can I play on Saturday?"

Teacher Yan looked at it for a long time, then turned and wrote a line on the blackboard: "What are called the joints are where the spirit-qi travels, goes out and comes in; they are not skin, flesh, sinew or bone." "The first chapter of the Lingshu. Needles can make it hurt a little less. They can't make that sinew of yours grow a little faster. Pain and injury are two separate ledgers. That sinew has to grow back on its own."

That night, Ahe came up to the sixth floor with bandages. She tossed the bandages on the desk, lifted one foot, shut her eyes, and stood on the concrete floor without a wobble: "Everyone who sprains an ankle has to do this. Ligaments heal slow, way slower than muscle. And a sprain hurts the nerves in your foot too — your brain stops knowing where your foot is, so you keep rolling it. Stand on one foot with your eyes shut every day, till you can do a minute without wobbling."

He tried it once, holding the edge of the desk. The moment he closed his eyes, he was a bamboo pole stuck in mud, both arms windmilling in the air; on the third second, his good foot slapped down onto the floor.

"Three seconds," said Ahe.
